paras: The killing of Stephen Wade was the night shooting of a sixty-year-old Black man at his home in a Black settlement near Palestine, Darke County, Ohio, by a band of twenty to thirty masked horsemen in October 1878. Wade and his family had been accused of thefts and ordered by red-ink notices to leave the county. Newspapers headlined it as "Ohio Ku-Klux", and men indicted for it were arrested in Indiana and Ohio and one was tried for murder in March 1879.

About a year earlier a man named Guyer had been shot at the door of his house in Palestine by a gang of masked horsemen, and no one was brought to justice. Wade and his family were "charged with stealing" by neighbors, and on June 14, 1878, a notice mailed from Winchester, Indiana, told Stephen, Robert, Benz. and Philip Wade to leave Darke County within thirty days. A second notice with a drawing of a coffin followed on September 14, and the family decided to move.

Near midnight on a Sunday, reported in a Greenville dispatch of October 7, 1878, armed and masked men on horseback surrounded Wade's house while his sons were away arranging the family's removal. A shot through the window smashed a mirror or clock above his bed, and the men called on him to come out. In the Dayton Journal's version Wade fired back before he went to the door, while the Chicago Times said he ran for the back door to escape. In both accounts he was hit in the face by a shotgun charge that entered his brain, and he died almost at once.
His housekeeper and three children came out of the house unhurt after the men left.

The coroner held an inquest, and a post-mortem removed sixteen shot from Wade's brain and thirty from his face, neck and body. No arrests were made at first, but by November seven Darke County "regulars" were reported held for kidnapping a son of Wade. In January 1879 a Wayne County, Indiana, marshal and Darke County officers arrested men from both sides of the state line whom a grand jury had indicted for kidnapping young Wade and murdering his father.

The Indiana State Sentinel named William Shumach, sixty, "of colored blood", as the principal suspect. Shumach told its correspondent that the "kidnapping" had been the arrest of William Wade for stealing a pig, and that he was at home ill on the night of the murder. The trial of William Shumake for Wade's murder opened at Greenville in March 1879 with two hundred witnesses, and no report of its outcome was found.

Wade's killing reached distant papers through competing Ohio accounts: a Chicago Times dispatch from Greenville, a Cincinnati Commercial special and a Dayton Journal interview with a farmer. The New Orleans Daily Democrat ran the Chicago Times story under "OHIO KUKLUX. A Negro Ordered Out of Darke County", and the Commercial later compared the county to Southern counties "where Ku-Klux law reigns supreme." The Jackson Standard opened its reprint with "Another nigger has been shot. It was again in Ohio," before an account that called the killing a "bloody outrage."

Coverage of the arrests took a different line, as the Sentinel called the accused a "gang of half-breed negroes" and described each prisoner by color. The killing came back into print in March 1881, when thirty-one Palestine residents were arrested for threatening saloon keeper Jacob Long, and the New York Sun recalled that "a negro named Stephen Wade was served in like manner" as Guyer. The Alexandria Gazette, reprinted in the Shepherdstown Register, said a Black man had "recently" been shot at his door and asked, "Suppose this state of affairs existed in a southern town?" Der Westbote told those arrests as a temperance raid on Long's saloon, though it tied his threat to the secret order it said had shot Guyer and Wade.

The Greenville dispatch and the trial report name the victim Stephen Wade, while the Cincinnati Commercial and Dayton Journal accounts, both from a farmer, call him Julius. The band numbered thirty in the Chicago Times and "fully twenty" in the Dayton Journal, and the house was placed twelve miles west or ten miles northeast of Greenville.

Wade was killed by a band of twenty to thirty masked men acting with no legal authority [A1][A3], after he and his family were accused of stealing and ordered to leave [A1][A2].
A Chicago Times dispatch from Greenville [A1] and separate Cincinnati Commercial and Dayton Journal accounts [A2][A3] agree on the killing, and a murder trial followed [A7].

accounts.label: Chicago Times dispatch from Greenville
accounts.gist: Thirty masked horsemen surrounded Stephen Wade's house in a Black settlement, fired in, and shot him in the left eye as he ran for the back door; he and his family had been charged with stealing and ordered out by notice.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Commercial and Dayton Journal (local farmer)
accounts.gist: 'Julius Wade', accused of thefts and warned by red-ink letters, exchanged shots with about twenty masked men and was shot in the face when he opened the door.

accounts.label: Accused man's statement (William Shumach)
accounts.gist: Shumach said the 'kidnapping' was a lawful arrest of Wade's son for pig theft and that he was home ill the night of the murder.

accounts.label: 1881 retrospective
accounts.gist: Reports of the 1881 Palestine arrests said a regulator band had killed Guyer and then the Black man Stephen Wade.

framing.detail: The Chicago Times dispatch, reprinted under 'OHIO KUKLUX. A Negro Ordered Out of Darke County' in New Orleans, called it a 'cold-blooded and horrible murder' by a 'secret organization of a desperate character'.
The Jackson Standard opened its Dayton Journal reprint with 'Another nigger has been shot. It was again in Ohio,' then printed an account calling it a 'bloody outrage'.
The Cincinnati Commercial, reprinted as 'OHIO KU-KLUX', said Darke County 'might well entitle it to a high rank in those counties of the South where Ku-Klux law reigns supreme'.
The Indiana State Sentinel cast the arrests as vindicating the law against a 'gang of half-breed negroes' and described the prisoners by color.
In 1881 the Alexandria Gazette used the Palestine 'reign of mob law' as a sectional retort: 'Suppose this state of affairs existed in a southern town?'

conflicts.note: The Greenville Chicago Times dispatch, the indictment-era reports and the trial report all say Stephen; the Commercial and Dayton Journal versions both rest on a farmer's account.
Both describe masked men on horseback.

info: Near midnight on a Sunday, reported in a Greenville dispatch dated October 7, 1878 (i.e., the night of October 6, 1878); the trial report says 'October last'

Wade's house in a Black ('negro') settlement about twelve miles west of Greenville, four miles from where Guyer was killed at Palestine (Chicago Times); 'ten miles northeast of Greenville' (Dayton Journal); 'five or six miles from Palestine' (Cincinnati Commercial); 'an old log house' twelve miles from Greenville (trial report)
Stephen Wade, a 'colored' man aged sixty (Chicago Times, trial report, 1881 Sun); named 'Julius Wade' in the Cincinnati Commercial and Dayton Journal accounts
Wade and his family were 'charged with stealing' / accused of petty thefts in the neighborhood; no court charge against Stephen Wade is reported

A mob of armed, masked men on horseback, described as a secret organization or gang; men later charged were from a settlement on the Ohio-Indiana line the Indiana State Sentinel called 'half-breed negroes', plus at least one white man
